open.kicker: The method, in the school’s words
open.heading:
In all areas
{{of teaching.}}
body: Three things, and none of them a timetabled slot. There is no collaboration lesson and no multiple-intelligence week — the claim is that all three run through ordinary teaching, which is a harder thing to promise and a harder thing to fake.

three.heading:
Named, and each one
{{anchored to something}}
body: A method is only worth reading if each part of it points at something checkable. All three of Sunbeam’s do — two to the Principal’s own published words, and one to a certification held by a hundred members of staff.

collab.kicker: What collaboration looks like when it is real
collab.heading:
One basket
{{of thread.}}
body: The word “collaborative” survives on most school sites without ever touching a photograph. Here it does.
In the school’s own embroidery session the students are not each issued a kit — they work from **one shared basket of thread**, which means the thing a child needs next is in somebody else’s hand.
The cooking activity is built the same way: one demonstration table, a class in paper chef hats around it, and no version of the task that can be completed alone.
Neither is a lesson called Collaboration. That is the school’s point — it is in the shape of an ordinary activity rather than in a slot on the timetable.

plat.kicker: And the second of the three
plat.heading:
Different talents,
{{different platforms.}}
body: “All the students do not have the same talents” is easy to say and expensive to act on — acting on it means running enough different things that a child who is not academic still has somewhere to be good. The school’s own published record is the evidence.

close.heading:
Three things,
{{everywhere.}}
body: The school publishes its method, the Principal’s words behind two of the three, and the certification behind the first. It does not publish lesson plans, a scheme of work, or an observation framework — so no lesson shape is described here.
